Differentially Private Range Subgraph Counting

Xian Chen Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China    Ruobing Bai Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China    Pan Peng Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Technology, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, China Correspondence to:ppeng@ustc.edu.cn
Abstract

Subgraph counting is a fundamental problem in graph analysis. Motivated by practical scenarios where graph analytics are performed on subgraphs induced by selected vertices – rather than on the entire graph – and by growing privacy concerns, we initiate the study of differentially private range subgraph counting (DPRSC). The goal is to privately count occurrences of a fixed pattern graph within induced subgraphs defined by multi-dimensional attribute ranges. Unlike classical point counting, subgraph counting is inherently nonlinear and exhibits high sensitivity: a single edge modification can affect many subgraph occurrences. We present the first efficient algorithms for DPRSC with small additive error. Our approach introduces a subgraph projection that reduces DPRSC to weighted orthogonal range counting, enabling the use of range trees and local sensitivity estimation to achieve accurate private query answering. We complement our algorithms with matching lower bounds, obtained by reducing reconstruction attacks to DPRSC and leveraging discrepancy theory. In particular, we show that any differentially private algorithm for DPRSC must incur additive error exponential in the dimension. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our algorithms significantly outperform baseline methods in accuracy and runtime while maintaining strong privacy guarantees.

1 Introduction

Subgraph counting is essential for understanding the properties of a data graph and has been extensively studied (14; 1; 6; 16; 3; 27). Given a host graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and a pattern graph HH, a subgraph of GG that is isomorphic to HH is called an occurrence of HH. The goal is to compute the number of such occurrences. Subgraph counts serve as key graph statistics: for instance, triangles and kk-stars are central to computing the clustering coefficient, which are widely used to evaluate social and recommendation networks, while counting four-cycles is particularly informative for capturing clustering behavior in bipartite graphs such as online dating and mentor-student networks.

In many applications, beyond counting subgraphs in the entire graph, we are often interested in counting subgraphs within specific induced subgraphs determined by vertex attributes. For instance, in patient or social networks, analysts may wish to count patterns among individuals within certain age ranges or geographic regions. In financial networks, counting transaction patterns among entities with similar risk profiles or locations can help identify fraudulent activities or assess systemic risks. More generally, vertices often carry multidimensional attributes, and practitioners seek to issue repeated subgraph-counting queries restricted to vertices whose attributes fall within specified ranges.

Motivated by these scenarios, we introduce the Range Subgraph Counting problem that combines classical subgraph counting with multidimensional range queries over vertex attributes.

Definition 1.1 (Range Subgraph Counting (RSC)).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an nn-vertex undirected graph, where each vertex v∈Vv\in V is associated with an attribute vector 𝐚⁡(v)∈ℝd\mathbf{a}(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a query range q=[ℓ1,r1]×⋯×[ℓd,rd]q=[\ell_{1},r_{1}]\times\dots\times[\ell_{d},r_{d}], define

Vq={v∈V∣ℓi≤ai(v)≤ri,i∈[d]}.V_{q}=\{v\in V\mid\ell_{i}\leq a_{i}(v)\leq r_{i},i\in[d]\}.

Let Gq=G⁡[Vq]G_{q}=G[V_{q}] denote the subgraph of GG induced by VqV_{q}.

Let HH be a fixed connected pattern graph with O⁡(1)O(1) vertices and let QQ be a set of query ranges. The goal is to return, for each query q∈Qq\in Q, the number of occurrences of HH in GqG_{q}.

Note that vertex attributes may represent age, time or location, depending on the practical context. Additionally, an occurrence is only counted if all its vertices are contained within VqV_{q}. Prior work by 20 studied the 11-dimensional version of this problem, focusing on optimizing the trade-off between space and query time.

Differential privacy perspective In this work, we study the range subgraph counting problem from the perspective of differential privacy (DP). DP enables meaningful statistical analysis while ensuring that the presence or absence of any single individual’s data has a limited impact on the output (22). We focus on edge DP. Two graphs GG and G′G^{\prime} with the same node set VV are said to be neighboring, denoted G∼G′G\sim G^{\prime}, if they differ by exactly one edge. (A stronger notion, known as node DP, has also been studied; see, e.g., (8; 13; 37).) Throughout this work, vertex attributes are assumed to be public.

Definition 1.2 (Edge DP (43)).

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1). A randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP if for all measurable events SS in the output space of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and all neighboring graph G∼G′G\sim G^{\prime},

Pr[𝒜(G)∈S]≤eεPr[𝒜(G′)∈S]+δ.\Pr[\mathcal{A}(G)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{A}(G^{\prime})\in S]+\delta.

When δ=0\delta=0, we say that 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies pure DP (or ε\varepsilon-DP); when 0<δ<10<\delta<1, it satisfies approximate DP.

Let fH​(G)f_{H}(G) denote the number of occurrences of HH in GG. A fundamental property of DP implies that any edge-DP algorithm for subgraph counting must incur additive error proportional to the local sensitivity LSfH​(G)\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G) with constant probability (38). Classical DP mechanisms instead depend on the global sensitivity GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}, which can be significantly larger. Various alternatives to global sensitivity – often via instance-dependent sensitivity bounds – have been proposed, e.g., smooth sensitivity, ladder functions, and private higher-order local sensitivity (43; 49; 42). While DP subgraph counting on the entire graph has been studied extensively, private algorithms for range subgraph counting have remained unexplored.

The challenge in range subgraph counting is twofold. First, subgraph counts already exhibit high sensitivity, even without range restrictions. Second, range queries require answering subgraph counts over many induced subgraphs GqG_{q}, leading to increased algorithmic and privacy complexity that depends on the size of the query set QQ. A naive approach – privately answering each query independently by adding Laplace noise – results in prohibitive error due to sensitivity scaling with |Vq||V_{q}| and privacy loss accumulating via composition. When |Q|=Θ⁡(n2​d)|Q|=\Theta(n^{2d}), the resulting error can overwhelm the true signal, even for simple patterns such as triangles. Moreover, range subgraph counting is inherently nonlinear, preventing the direct application of DP techniques developed for linear query workloads.

We present a simple polynomial-time ε\varepsilon-DP algorithm with an additive error O⁡(n​log⁡(n​|Q|)​GSfH)O(n\sqrt{\log(n|Q|)}\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}) for any dd and constant ε\varepsilon based on randomized response (see Theorem H.6). We further extend an approach in 25 to obtain an instance-dependent error for any dd and HH (see Theorem H.7). Since in Theorem 1.4, the exponent of nn multiplied in front of HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G) is always less than 11, this result provides a stronger lower bound than Theorem 1.4 when dd is sufficiently large.

1.2 Technical overview

A natural approach is to reduce range subgraph counting to a DP range point counting problem by embedding vertices into a Euclidean space, and then applying existing DP algorithms for orthogonal range counting (see, e.g., 24). However, unlike point counting, subgraph counting is inherently nonlinear: the sum of occurrences of a pattern graph in two graphs is not necessarily equal to the number of occurrences in their union, and a single edge change can affect many subgraphs (e.g., one edge may participate in Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) triangles), leading to high sensitivity.

To address these challenges, we introduce a subgraph projection technique that maps each occurrence of the pattern graph HH to a point in ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} based on vertex attributes, converting range subgraph counting into estimating weighted point counts over axis-aligned rectangles. The weight of each point corresponds to the number of occurrences associated with the underlying vertex tuple. A single edge can change the weights of all points projected by the subgraphs it is associated with. We organize these points using a range tree (5; 24) and add Laplace noise to node weights, allowing each query to be answered by aggregating a small number of tree nodes. This approach effectively leverages query correlations and substantially reduces noise. Finally, to further improve accuracy, we adapt the local sensitivity estimation technique of 42 and incorporate it into the range tree, yielding smaller additive error.

To complement our algorithms, we establish lower bounds on the additive error for differentially private range subgraph counting via a reduction from the reconstruction attacks (RA) problem, inspired by the framework of 40. Given an RA instance 𝐱\mathbf{x}, together with a point set P⊆ℝdP\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and a query set QQ with non-empty common intersection, we construct a Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n)-vertex graph G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) whose private edges encode the entries of 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Any DP algorithm for RSC on (G⁡(𝐱),Q)(G(\mathbf{x}),Q) can then be transformed into a DP algorithm for RA.

The lower bound follows from two key ingredients: (i) known lower bounds for DP reconstruction attacks, and (ii) the existence of point sets PP and query families QQ whose incidence matrices have large discrepancy (Lemma 2.10). Our main technical contribution shows that the discrepancy of a matrix associated with the RSC instance (G⁡(𝐱),Q)(G(\mathbf{x}),Q) is larger by a factor of Θ⁡(GSfH)\Theta(\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}) (Lemma 4.3). The proof relies on an approximate reduction and a careful classification of subgraphs according to the number of private edges they contain. Combining this discrepancy bound with standard connections between discrepancy and differential privacy completes the lower bound argument.

Due to space constraint, we defer the discussion of other related work to Appendix B.

Differential privacy The global sensitivity and local sensitivity of a function are defined as follows.

Definition 2.1 (Local Sensitivity (43)).

For any function f:𝒳→ℝkf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{k} defined over a domain space 𝒳\mathcal{X} and any G∈𝒳G\in\mathcal{X}, the local sensitivity of the function ff at input GG is defined as LSf(G)=maxG′:G∼G′‖f(G)−f(G′)‖1.\mathrm{LS}_{f}(G)=\max_{G^{\prime}:G\sim G^{\prime}}\left\|f(G)-f(G^{\prime})\right\|_{1}.

Definition 2.2 (Global Sensitivity (22)).

For any function f:𝒳→ℝkf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{k} defined over a domain space 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the global sensitivity of the function ff is defined as GSf=maxG∼G′⁡‖f⁡(G)−f⁡(G′)‖1=maxG⁡LSf​(G).\mathrm{GS}_{f}=\max_{G\sim G^{\prime}}\left\|f(G)-f(G^{\prime})\right\|_{1}=\max_{G}\mathrm{LS}_{f}(G).

We will make use of the following composition theorems of differential privacy.

Proposition 2.3 (Basic Composition Theorem (22)).

For any ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0, the composition of kk (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private algorithms is (k​ε,k​δ)(k\varepsilon,k\delta)-differentially private.

Proposition 2.4 (Advanced Composition Theorem (34)).

For any ε,δ,δ′>0\varepsilon,\delta,\delta^{\prime}>0, the composition of kk (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private algorithms is (k​ε2/2+ε​2​k​ln⁡(1/δ′),k​δ+δ′)(k\varepsilon^{2}/2+\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta^{\prime})},k\delta+\delta^{\prime})-differentially private.

We say a zero-mean random variable XX follows the Laplace distribution with parameter b if the probability density function of XX follows Lap⁡(b)=12​b​e−|x|b\mathrm{Lap}(b)=\frac{1}{2b}e^{-\frac{|x|}{b}}.

Fact 2.6.

If Y∼Lap⁡(b)Y\sim\mathrm{Lap}(b), then Pr[|Y|>tb]≤e−t\Pr[|Y|>tb]\leq e^{-t}.

Definition 2.7 (Laplace Mechanism (22)).

For any function f:𝒳→ℝkf:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{k}, the Laplace mechanism on input x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} samples 𝒴1,…,𝒴k\mathcal{Y}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{Y}_{k} independently from Lap⁡(GSfε)\mathrm{Lap}(\frac{\mathrm{GS}_{f}}{\varepsilon}) and outputs M⁡(x)=f⁡(x)+(𝒴1,…,𝒴k)M(x)=f(x)+(\mathcal{Y}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{Y}_{k}). The Laplace mechanism is ε\varepsilon-DP.

3 The Upper Bound

Our approximate DP algorithm in Theorem 1.3 is based on a pure DP algorithm, which we introduce below.

3.1 The pure DP algorithm

The high level description of the algorithm is as follows: (1) Find all occurrences of subgraph HH in GG and map each to a rank tuple (see below) in [n]2​d[n]^{2d}. Project each occurrence into its rank tuple to obtain a weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} of length n2​dn^{2d} (see Algorithm 1). (2) Treat the rank tuples weighted points in [n]2​d[n]^{2d} and build a differentially private 2​d2dD range tree over them (see Algorithm 2). (3) Answer each query by traversing the range tree and aggregating the noisy weights of the corresponding nodes (see Algorithm 3).

Now we describe our algorithm in more detail.

Subgraph counting projection Algorithm 1 takes as input an nn-vertex graph G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}). For each i∈[d]i\in[d], let Ai​(V,𝐚)A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a}) be the set of the ii-th attributes for all vertices in VV. Let si​(v)∈[n]s_{i}(v)\in[n] represent the rank of 𝐚i​(v)\mathbf{a}_{i}(v) in Ai​(V,𝐚)A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a}) for some vertex vv, when the ii-th attributes in Ai​(V,𝐚)A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a}) are sorted in ascending order. Note that we have si​(u)=si​(v)s_{i}(u)=s_{i}(v) if two vertices uu and vv have the same ii-th attribute. Now we present the definition of the rank tuple of an occurrence.

Definition 3.1 (Rank Tuple).

The rank tuple of an occurrence H′=(V⁡(H′),E⁡(H′))H^{\prime}=(V(H^{\prime}),E(H^{\prime})) is defined as a 2​d2d-tuple (si​(ui),si​(vi))i=1d(s_{i}(u_{i}),s_{i}(v_{i}))_{i=1}^{d} satisfying ui=arg⁡minv∈V⁡(H′)​si​(v)u_{i}=\arg\min_{v\in V(H^{\prime})}s_{i}(v) and vi=arg⁡maxv∈V⁡(H′)​si​(v)v_{i}=\arg\max_{v\in V(H^{\prime})}s_{i}(v) for all i∈[d]i\in[d].

For each occurrence of a subgraph HH in GG, it updates a weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} at the position corresponding to its rank tuple. Each position in 𝐰\mathbf{w} records the number of occurrences that share a specific rank tuple.

DP range tree construction Algorithm 2 takes as input the project vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} from Algorithm 1. Then the algorithm treats each rank tuple 𝐯\mathbf{v} in [n]2​d[n]^{2d} as a point with weight 𝐰𝐯\mathbf{w}_{\mathbf{v}} and utilizes a 2​d2dD range tree (see Section C.1) to preprocess these points.

The schematic diagram of the 2​d2dD range tree, with d=1d=1 as an example, is shown in Figure 1. In the 2​d2dD range tree, each leaf node of every 11D range tree corresponds to a point in [n]2​d[n]^{2d}, and its weight is set to the weight of the corresponding point. The weight of each internal node of every 11D range tree is set to the sum of the weights of its children. We add Laplace noise to the weights of nodes in all 11D range trees to ensure privacy.

Query procedure For any query q=∏i=1d[ℓi,ri]∈Qq=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[\ell_{i},r_{i}]\in Q, we first apply the discretization described below to obtain a new query q′q^{\prime}. Note that the ranges qq and q′q^{\prime} correspond to the same induced subgraph. For simplicity, we will use q=∏i=1d[ℓi,ri]q=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[\ell_{i},r_{i}] to refer to the discretized query.

Definition 3.2 (Discretization).

Let q=∏i=1d[ℓi,ri]q=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[\ell_{i},r_{i}] be a query. For each [li,ri][l_{i},r_{i}], we associate it with two vertices vℓiv_{\ell_{i}} and vriv_{r_{i}}, where vℓi=arg⁡minv∈V,𝐚i​(v)≥ℓi​𝐚i​(v)v_{\ell_{i}}=\arg\min_{v\in V,\mathbf{a}_{i}(v)\geq\ell_{i}}\mathbf{a}_{i}(v) and vri=arg⁡maxv∈V,𝐚i​(v)≤ri​𝐚i​(v)v_{r_{i}}=\arg\max_{v\in V,\mathbf{a}_{i}(v)\leq r_{i}}\mathbf{a}_{i}(v). The discretized query q′q^{\prime} is defined as ∏i=1d[si​(vℓi),si​(vri)]\prod_{i=1}^{d}[s_{i}(v_{\ell_{i}}),s_{i}(v_{r_{i}})].

For a discretized query q=∏i=1d[ℓi,ri]q=\prod_{i=1}^{d}[\ell_{i},r_{i}], we call the 2​d2dD range tree query with range ∏i=1d([ℓi,n]×[1,ri])\prod_{i=1}^{d}([\ell_{i},n]\times[1,r_{i}]), which ensures that all subgraphs exactly falling within the range are counted in the answer.

The complete algorithm is presented in Algorithm 3, with its analysis deferred to Section E.1. To improve time efficiency, the implementation of Algorithm 3 differs slightly from the pseudocode without affecting correctness (see Section E.3). As a result, we obtain the following theorem.

Theorem 3.3 (Pure DPRSC).

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an ε\varepsilon-DP algorithm that, given a graph G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}) with dd-dimensional vertex attributes, a fixed pattern graph HH, and a query set QQ, outputs noisy answers f~H​(Gq)\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q}) which satisfy maxq∈Q⁡|fH​(Gq)−f~H​(Gq)|=O⁡(GSfH⋅log⁡(n​|Q|)⋅log3​d⁡nε)\max_{q\in Q}\left|f_{H}(G_{q})-\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})\right|=O\left(\frac{\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot\sqrt{\log(n|Q|)}\cdot\log^{3d}{n}}{\varepsilon}\right), with probability ≥1−1n\geq 1-\frac{1}{n}. Here, the hidden constants are of the form cO⁡(d)c^{O(d)} for some universal constant c>1c>1.

3.2 The approximate DP algorithm

Now we present our approximate DP algorithm. We begin by introducing some notation. Let S⊆V×VS\subseteq V\times V be a set of vertex pairs. Let fH​(G,S)f_{H}(G,S) denote the number of occurrences of a fixed pattern graph HH containing all edges in SS in the graph (V⁡(G),E⁡(G)∪S)(V(G),E(G)\cup S). We define fH(k)​(G)=max|S|=k⁡fH​(G,S)f^{(k)}_{H}(G)=\max_{|S|=k}f_{H}(G,S). Note that we have fH(1)​(G)=LSfH​(G)f_{H}^{(1)}(G)=\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G) by definition.

The local sensitivity of 𝐰\mathbf{w} is estimated by iteratively adding noise to ensure privacy (see Algorithm 4). The approach is derived from 42, whose method was originally designed to estimate subgraph counts but has been modified here to estimate the local sensitivity.

The complete approximate DP algorithm is presented in Algorithm 5. It closely resembles the pure DP one (i.e. Algorithm 3), with the key difference being in the parameter settings. The algorithm adds noise in the range tree based on the private estimation of local sensitivity rather than global sensitivity. The analysis of this algorithm (i.e., proof of Theorem 1.3) and the implementation details are deferred to Sections E.2 and E.3, respectively.

4 The Lower Bound

In this section, we prove the following theorem which presents a lower bound for DPRSC.

Theorem 4.1 (Lower Bound of DPRSC).

For any pattern graph HH, let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm with constants ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈[0,12)\delta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}) for the range subgraph counting problem with additive error η=maxq∈Q⁡|fH​(Gq)−f~H​(Gq)|\eta=\max_{q\in Q}|f_{H}(G_{q})-\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})| with a sufficiently large constant success probability.

Then there exist infinitely many nn-vertex graphs G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}) with dd-dimensional vertex attributes and a corresponding query set QQ, such that

  • •

    if d=O⁡(1)d=O(1), then η=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n¯⋅GSfH)\eta=\Omega(\log^{d-1}\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}});

  • •

    if d=O⁡(log⁡n¯)d=O(\log\bar{n}), then η=2Ω⁡(d)​GSfH\eta=2^{\Omega(d)}\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}};

  • •

    if d=Ω⁡(log⁡n¯)d=\Omega(\log\bar{n}), then η=n¯Ω⁡(1)​GSfH\eta=\bar{n}^{\Omega(1)}\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}};

where n¯=min⁡(n,|Q|)\bar{n}=\min(n,|Q|) can be arbitrarily large.

We prove Theorem 4.1 via a reduction from the reconstruction attacks (RA) problem to DPRSC, using techniques inspired by 40. Moreover, the proof reveals that for the constructed hard instances, the approximated local sensitivity HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G) is, with high probability, within a constant factor of the global sensitivity GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}. This directly implies Theorem 1.4, whose full proof is deferred to Section F.3.

In Section F.4, we further provide a lower bound of η=Ω⁡(log⁡n¯⋅GSfH)\eta=\Omega(\log\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}) for the case d=1d=1, under the additional assumption that δ=n−Ω⁡(1)\delta=n^{-\Omega(1)}.

4.1 The reduction

We first introduce the reconstruction attacks problem and then reduce it to range subgraph counting.

Definition 4.2 (Reconstruction Attacks (RA); (21)).

Given a private vector 𝐱∈{0,1}N\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{N}, a reconstruction algorithm outputs a vector in {0,1}N\{0,1\}^{N}. The goal is to design an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm ℬ\mathcal{B} minimizing ‖ℬ⁡(𝐱)−𝐱‖1\|\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}.

From RA to RSC Let P⊆ℝdP\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a point set of size nn and let QQ be a collection of mm axis-parallel boxes B1,…,BmB_{1},\dots,B_{m} with a non-empty common intersection.

Graph construction We construct a graph G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) as follows. Create two copies of PP, denoted P(1)P^{(1)} and P(2)P^{(2)}. For each p∈Pp\in P, let p(1)∈P(1)p^{(1)}\in P^{(1)} and p(2)∈P(2)p^{(2)}\in P^{(2)} denote its copies. Let WW be a set of n−2n-2 auxiliary vertices, all lying in the common intersection of the boxes in QQ.

The vertex set of G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) is V=P(1)∪P(2)∪WV=P^{(1)}\cup P^{(2)}\cup W, so that |V|=3​n−2|V|=3n-2 (see Figure 2). For each p∈Pp\in P, we add an edge between p(1)p^{(1)} and p(2)p^{(2)} if and only if xp=1x_{p}=1. In addition, every vertex in P(1)∪P(2)P^{(1)}\cup P^{(2)} is connected to every vertex in WW, and WW induces a clique.

The edges between p(1)p^{(1)} and p(2)p^{(2)} encode the private data 𝐱\mathbf{x}, while all other edges are public. Consequently, two vectors 𝐱,𝐱′\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime} are neighboring if and only if the corresponding graphs G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) and G⁡(𝐱′)G(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) are neighboring.

Hard instance We begin with a point set of size n¯\bar{n} and a query set QQ from Lemma 2.10. We then add n−n¯n-\bar{n} dummy points lying outside all boxes in QQ to form PP. Using this point set PP and query set QQ, we construct the graph G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) as described above and use QQ as the query set for the RSC problem. We denote the resulting instance by (G⁡(𝐱),Q)(G(\mathbf{x}),Q), which completes the construction of the hard instance.

4.2 The analysis

To prove the lower bound using the constructed instance (G⁡(𝐱),Q)(G(\mathbf{x}),Q), we associate it with a matrix 𝐀H\mathbf{A}_{H} and show that this matrix has large discrepancy.

The matrix The matrix 𝐀H\mathbf{A}_{H} is defined with respect to the complete graph K3​n−2K_{3n-2} on vertex set V=P(1)∪P(2)∪WV=P^{(1)}\cup P^{(2)}\cup W. It has |Q||Q| rows and fH​(K3​n−2)f_{H}(K_{3n-2}) columns. Each row corresponds to a query q∈Qq\in Q, i.e., the induced subgraph K3​n−2​[Vq]K_{3n-2}[V_{q}], and each column corresponds to an occurrence H′H^{\prime} of the pattern HH in K3​n−2K_{3n-2}. The entries are defined as

(AH)q,H′={1,if ​E​(H′)⊆E⁡(K3​n−2​[Vq]);0,otherwise.(A_{H})_{q,H^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }E(H^{\prime})\subseteq E(K_{3n-2}[V_{q}]);\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Note that 𝐀H\mathbf{A}_{H} is fixed and depends only on K3​n−2K_{3n-2} and the query set QQ, and is independent of the edge set of G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}).

Let 𝐱H∈{0,1}fH​(K3​n−2)\mathbf{x}_{H}\in\{0,1\}^{f_{H}(K_{3n-2})} be the indicator vector whose coordinates correspond to occurrences H′H^{\prime} of HH in K3​n−2K_{3n-2}, where (𝐱H)H′=1(\mathbf{x}_{H})_{H^{\prime}}=1 if all edges of H′H^{\prime} are present in G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}), and 00 otherwise. Then for each query q∈Qq\in Q, the quantity (𝐀H​𝐱H)q(\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}_{H})_{q} equals the number of occurrences of HH in the induced subgraph (G​(𝐱))​[Vq](G(\mathbf{x}))[V_{q}].

Let Cα,HC_{\alpha,H} denote the set of vectors χ=𝐱H−𝐱H′∈{0,±1}fH​(K3​n−2)\chi=\mathbf{x}_{H}-\mathbf{x}_{H}^{\prime}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{f_{H}(K_{3n-2})} such that 𝐱−𝐱′∈Cα\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in C_{\alpha}. The following lemma, proved in Section F.1, shows that 𝐀H\mathbf{A}_{H} inherits large discrepancy from the point-incidence matrix.

Lemma 4.3.

Let P⊆ℝdP\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a set of nn points, and let QQ be a collection of mm sets B1,…,Bm⊆ℝdB_{1},\dots,B_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} with a non-empty common intersection. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} be the incidence matrix of {Bj∩P:j∈[m]}\{B_{j}\cap P:j\in[m]\}. For any α=Ω⁡(1)\alpha=\Omega(1) and any pattern graph HH, if discCα​(𝐀)=ω​(1)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=\omega(1), then discCα,H​(𝐀H)=Ω⁡(GSfH⋅discCα​(𝐀))\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H})=\Omega\!\left(\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})\right), where GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} denotes the global sensitivity of fHf_{H} on nn-vertex graphs.

Proof sketch of Theorem 4.1 Given the above reduction, we show that if there exists a DP algorithm for RSC whose additive error is asymptotically smaller than discCα,H​(𝐀H)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}), then this algorithm can be used to solve RA with small error (Lemma F.2). This contradicts known lower bounds for RA (Lemma F.3), and thus yields the desired lower bound for DPRSC. We defer the full argument to Section F.2.

5 Experiments

Now we present our experimental results. All algorithms were implemented in Python22 2 The corresponding codes and data are available at https://github.com/Airleave/DPRSC., and run on an Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8562Y Processor @ 2.80 GHZ with 768 GB RAM. We evaluated our methods on three real-world datasets, after removing self-loops and duplicate edges from each graph. Basic statistics for these datasets are summarized in Table 1. The edges are treated as sensitive data.

Baseline There is no prior work on DP range subgraph counting. We construct two natural baselines for comparison. The first baseline PDP_Comp answers each query independently by adding Laplace noise with scale GSfH⋅|Q|ε\frac{\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot|Q|}{\varepsilon}, using the basic composition theorem (Proposition 2.3). The second baseline ADP_Comp improves upon this by applying Lemma E.5 and the advanced composition theorem (Proposition 2.4), adding Laplace noise with scale Θ⁡(HS~fH​(G)⋅|Q|​ln⁡(1/δ)ε)\Theta(\frac{\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G)\cdot\sqrt{|Q|\ln(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}). We denote our pure DP algorithm (Algorithm 3) and approximate DP algorithm (Algorithm 5) by PDP_RSC and ADP_RSC, respectively. The comparison of different algorithms is provided in Table 2.

Setting and metric All algorithms satisfy either ε\varepsilon-DP or (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP. We set ε=2.0,δ=10−5\varepsilon=2.0,\delta=10^{-5} (which satisfies δ<1n\delta<\frac{1}{n} for all datasets considered), d=1d=1 and |Q|=⌈n1.5⌉|Q|=\lceil n^{1.5}\rceil by default. Each query qq in QQ is generated randomly and corresponds to an induced vertex set VqV_{q} with |Vq|=Θ⁡(n)|V_{q}|=\Theta(n). Experiments are conducted on three datasets, with HH being a triangle, 2-star, or edge. Results for edge and CA-Netscience are deferred to Sections G.1 and G.2, respectively. For each vertex in these networks, we independently sample attributes from a standard normal distribution as a conservative (worst-case) evaluation; the rationale for this choice is provided in Section G.4. We also include additional experiments to complement the default setting: Results for d>1d>1, small-range queries and real attributes are provided in Sections G.2, G.3 and G.4, respectively. We measure relative error as |f~H​(Gq)−fH​(Gq)|max⁡(fH​(Gq),0.001​n)\frac{|\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})-f_{H}(G_{q})|}{\max(f_{H}(G_{q}),0.001n)}, following standard practice (31). Each algorithm is run at least 20 times; we report mean relative error and runtime, with standard-deviation bands shown in figures. We define the query time as the time required to answer a single query, the total query time as the sum of the query times over all queries, and the total time as the sum of the preprocessing time and the total query time.

Relative error vs. ε\varepsilon Figure 6 shows that our algorithms consistently outperform the baselines across all tested privacy parameter ε\varepsilon (smaller values of ε\varepsilon correspond to stronger privacy guarantees), achieving substantially lower mean error and variance. The approximate DP algorithm ADP_RSC generally performs best on sparse graphs, except for 2-stars on Wiki-Squirrel, where large dmaxd_{\max} increases the local sensitivity and noise relative to PDP_RSC, since HS~fH​(G)≈2​dmax\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G)\approx 2d_{\max} for 2-stars (Section C.3). For triangles, ADP_RSC is more sensitive to small ε\varepsilon since estimating HS~fH\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}} requires iteratively adding noise related to ε\varepsilon and δ\delta.

Relative error vs. |Q||Q| As shown in Figure 6, our algorithms are largely insensitive to |Q||Q|, whereas baseline errors increase quickly with |Q||Q|. A minor exception occurs for very small |Q|<2​n|Q|<2n in the ADP_Comp vs. ADP_RSC comparison, consistent with the theoretical bounds in Theorem 1.3. The performance gap grows as |Q||Q| increases.

Runtime For runtime evaluation, we assume that the queries in QQ are i.i.d. and uniformly sampled from all queries that produce distinct induced subgraphs. We evaluated the relationship between the total time and |Q||Q| in Figure 6. |Q||Q| ranges from 1 to Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}), which corresponds to the full range of |Q||Q| under our setting when d=1d=1. Since exhaustively evaluating all Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) queries is computationally prohibitive, we sample a sufficiently large number of queries from the distribution defined above. We continue sampling until the average query time converges, as measured by a small relative standard error (below 5%5\%), and use the average query time and preprocessing time (shown in Figure 6) to estimate the total time. Given the substantial differences in query time between our algorithms and the baselines, the resulting estimation error is negligible. As shown in Figure 6, our algorithms significantly outperform the baselines in query time, achieving lower latency by 3 to 4 orders of magnitude at the cost of higher preprocessing time. Note that PDP_comp requires no preprocessing. Here, the baselines compute exact counts of 2-stars using a straightforward implementation in O⁡(m)O(m) time, while exact triangle counting is carried out using the widely adopted algorithm from 14. Figure 6 shows that our algorithm consistently outperforms the baselines in total time when |Q|=Ω⁡(n)|Q|=\Omega(n), and the advantage becomes increasingly pronounced as |Q||Q| grows. Moreover, the advantage is more significant on larger datasets. Overall, when Q=Θ⁡(n2)Q=\Theta(n^{2}), the total time is dominated by the total query time, yielding a speedup of 3 to 4 orders of magnitude.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we study the DPRSC problem and present the first efficient algorithms achieving small additive error. We complement these results with lower bounds showing an exponential dependence on the attribute dimension, nearly matching our upper bounds.

A limitation of our work is that our current algorithms do not address settings in which attribute information is sensitive and must be protected. Combining our techniques with existing methods (e.g., (24)) may yield upper and lower bounds in this setting. However, achieving general algorithms with optimal utility guarantees would likely require new ideas beyond our current approach. In addition, a gap remains between our upper and lower bounds in certain parameter regimes, leaving room for improvement in both analysis and algorithm design. Another interesting direction is to extend the RSC problem to more challenging settings, such as dynamic graphs where edges or attributes evolve over time, and alternative privacy models including local differential privacy and node-level differential privacy.

Appendix B Other Related Work

DP subgraph counting The DP subgraph counting problem is a topic that has been extensively studied, primarily for the entire graph GG. 43 improved the utility guarantees for triangle counting in differential privacy by incorporating instance-dependent noise. 35 extended the smooth sensitivity approach to kk-stars and proposed methods for computing local sensitivity to perform kk-triangle counting. 37 introduced a triangle counting algorithm under the node-DP framework. 49 developed ladder functions for various subgraph counting tasks. 42 focused on optimizing runtime by calculating approximate smooth sensitivity for graphs with certain properties, achieving both privacy and utility while reducing time complexity. Additionally, several studies have examined subgraph counting under the local DP model, such as 31; 32; 33; 25, while 28 studied DP subgraph counting in dynamic model.

DP range queries 40 present algorithms for the halfspace range counting problem under differential privacy, achieving good approximate accuracy in terms of average squared error. 19 propose an algorithm for counting queries and bottleneck queries on shortest paths while ensuring differential privacy. A closer examination of their model reveals that they effectively address a range counting problem on a graph. A cut query on a graph is a specialized form of range counting, where the range space includes all possible cuts. The cut query problem is widely studied in the field of differential privacy, with significant research dedicated to it (29; 7; 30; 2; 26; 17).

DP lower bound DP lower bounds are often motivated by reconstruction attacks (21), which show that answering too many queries accurately can leak sensitive information about the dataset. Building on this technique, 40 explore the connections between discrepancy theory and DP lower bound. In particular, they establish the first lower bound on the average squared error for the private range counting problem. Subsequent improvements in discrepancy results by 39 further strengthen the lower bound. Furthermore, based on the connections, 26 studied the lower bound for DP synthetic graph generation to approximate all cuts, while 44 extended this to triangle-motif cuts. Their approaches heavily rely on the randomness inherent in Erdős–Rényi graphs, which limits its applicability to range subgraph counting for moderate dd.

We will make use of the following post-processing property of differential privacy.

Proposition C.1 (Post-processing Property (22)).

Let MM: ℝd1→ℝd2\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}} be an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private mechanism and let hh: ℝd2→ℝd3\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}} be an arbitrary function. Then, the function g∘Mg\circ M: ℝd1→ℝd3\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}} is also (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private.

The sum of multiple variables that follow the Laplace distribution satisfies the following properties.

Then, for ν≥∑ibi2\nu\geq\sqrt{\sum_{i}b^{2}_{i}} and 0<λ<2​2​ν2b0<\lambda<\frac{2\sqrt{2}\nu^{2}}{b} for b=maxi⁡{bi}b=\max_{i}\{b_{i}\}, Pr[|∑iXi|≥λ]≤2⋅exp(−λ28​ν2)\Pr\left[|\sum_{i}X_{i}|\geq\lambda\right]\leq 2\cdot\exp(-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{8\nu^{2}}). C.1 Definitions and properties of range tree

A range tree is a binary tree structure designed for interval queries and summation. For clarity, we define the tree construction and query process to streamline the algorithm’s description. The construction of the range tree is based primarily on 5, with minor modifications.

We begin by introducing the basic 11D range tree.

Definition C.3 (11D Range Tree).

Given a set of points P={(xt,wt)}P=\left\{(x_{t},w_{t})\right\}, where each point has an xx-coordinate xtx_{t} and a weight wtw_{t}, the 11D range tree is constructed as follows:

  1. 1.

    Sort the points by xx-coordinates, denoted as x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}.

  2. 2.

    Begin building the tree recursively from the root node, where the interval spans from x1x_{1} to xnx_{n}.

  3. 3.

    For a given interval xl,…,xrx_{l},\dots,x_{r} corresponding to a tree node pp, set m​i​d=⌊l+r2⌋mid=\lfloor\frac{l+r}{2}\rfloor. Recursively construct the left child using points xl,…,xm​i​dx_{l},\dots,x_{mid} and the right child using points xm​i​d+1,…,xrx_{mid+1},\dots,x_{r}. If the interval contains only one kind of coordinate, terminate the recursion and set the weight of the current tree node to the sum of the weights of the points at the coordinate.

  4. 4.

    During backtracking, sum the weights of the left child and the right child as the weight of the current tree node:

    n​o​d​e​.weight=l​e​f​t​.weight+r​i​g​h​t​.weight.node\text{.weight}=left\text{.weight}+right\text{.weight}.
Definition C.4 (11D Range Tree Query).

Given a query range [l​o​w,h​i​g​h][low,high], start at the root node of the 1D range tree TT.

  1. 1.

    Start the recursive query from the root node of TT.

  2. 2.

    For the current n​o​d​enode, if n​o​d​enode falls within the range [l​o​w,h​i​g​h][low,high], return pp.weight. If l​o​wlow lies within the left child of pp, recursively query the left subtree; if h​i​g​h1high_{1} lies within the right child, recursively query the right subtree.

  3. 3.

    When backtracking, sum the results of the left child and the right child and return them.

Next, we introduce the kkD Range Tree (k≥k\geq 2).

Definition C.5 (kkD Range Tree Construction).

For a set of points P={((xti)i=1k,wt)}P=\left\{((x^{i}_{t})_{i=1}^{k},w_{t})\right\} where each point has coordinates (xti)i=1k(x^{i}_{t})_{i=1}^{k} and a weight wtw_{t}, the kkD range tree is constructed as follow:

  1. 1.

    Group the points by their first dimension, and sort each group by the first dimension, denoted as p1,…,pnp_{1},\dots,p_{n}.

  2. 2.

    Construct the kkD range tree T1T_{1} using p1,…,pnp_{1},\dots,p_{n} in a similar approach to the 11D range tree, partitioning the first dimension. Note that each node of T1T_{1} contains an associated (k−1)(k-1)D range tree T2T_{2} for the second dimension, recursively.

  3. 3.

    For each node in T1T_{1}, take the points covered by that node, group them by their second dimension, sort them, and construct a corresponding (k−1)(k-1)D range tree T2T_{2}.

Definition C.6 (kkD Range Tree Query).

Given a kk-dimensional query range ∏i=1k[l​o​wi,h​i​g​hi]\prod_{i=1}^{k}[low_{i},high_{i}] and kkD range tree T1T_{1}:

  1. 1.

    Start the recursive query from the root node of T1T_{1}.

  2. 2.

    For the current n​o​d​enode, if n​o​d​enode falls within the range [l​o​w1,h​i​g​h1][low_{1},high_{1}], perform a query ∏i=2k[l​o​wi,h​i​g​hi]\prod_{i=2}^{k}[low_{i},high_{i}] on T2T_{2} (call (k−1)(k-1)D tree query recursively). If l​o​w1low_{1} lies within the left child of n​o​d​enode, recursively query the left subtree; if h​i​g​h1high_{1} lies within the right child, recursively query the right subtree.

  3. 3.

    When backtracking, sum the results of the left child and the right child and return them.

We present construction and query time complexity of kkD range tree for any k≥1k\geq 1.

Lemma C.7 (Construction Time).

For any k≥1k\geq 1, the runtime of kkD range tree construction is O⁡(n​logk​n)O(n\log^{k}{n}).

Lemma C.8 (Query Time).

For any k≥1k\geq 1, the runtime of kkD range tree query is O⁡(logk⁡n)O(\log^{k}{n}).

Based on the properties of the range tree, we can derive the following lemma.

Lemma C.9.

Let TT denote a kkD range tree constructed from a set of points P={((xti)i=1k,wt)}P=\{((x_{t}^{i})_{i=1}^{k},w_{t})\}. If a kk-dimensional query range ∏i=1k[l​o​wi,h​i​g​hi]\prod_{i=1}^{k}[low_{i},high_{i}] satisfies l​o​wi≤minx∈P⁡xilow_{i}\leq\min_{x\in P}x^{i} or h​i​g​hi≥maxx∈P⁡xihigh_{i}\geq\max_{x\in P}x^{i} for all i∈[k]i\in[k], the query result is the sum of the weights of at most ⌈log⁡n⌉k\lceil\log n\rceil^{k} tree nodes.

Proof.

Note that the depth of the tree (i.e., the maximum number of nodes along the path from the root node to any node in the tree) in each dimension of the kkD range tree is at most (⌈log⁡n⌉+1)(\lceil\log n\rceil+1) by Definition C.5. For each i∈[k]i\in[k], consider the process of querying the range [l​o​wi,h​i​g​hi][low_{i},high_{i}] on the (k−i+1)(k-i+1)D range trees.

If l​o​wi≤minx∈P⁡xilow_{i}\leq\min_{x\in P}x^{i} and h​i​g​hi≥maxx∈P⁡xihigh_{i}\geq\max_{x\in P}x^{i}, only the root node of each (k−i+1)(k-i+1)D range tree can be queried. Otherwise, the weight of the root node is not included in the sum. Moreover, when querying the left and right subtrees simultaneously on each (k−i+1)(k-i+1)D range tree, at least one of the subtrees will return after performing a query at its root node. Therefore, for each 11D range tree, at most ⌈log⁡n⌉\lceil\log n\rceil tree nodes’ weights are summed; For each (k−i+1)(k-i+1)D range tree satisfying 2≤i≤k2\leq i\leq k, at most ⌈log⁡n⌉\lceil\log n\rceil tree nodes will be queried.

After aggregating the results over kk dimensions, the query result is the sum of the weights of at most ⌈log⁡n⌉k\lceil\log n\rceil^{k} tree nodes. ∎

C.2 Tight bound on the global sensitivity of subgraph counting

In Section 3, we used GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} to denote the global sensitivity of subgraph counting. We present an exact method for computing the global sensitivity GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}, from which we derive a simple and asymptotically tight bound. Table 3 summarizes the global sensitivity of common pattern graphs.

Definition C.10 (Automorphism Group).

An automorphism of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a permutation σ\sigma of VV such that (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E if and only if (σ⁡(u),σ⁡(v))∈E(\sigma(u),\sigma(v))\in E. The set of all automorphisms of GG forms a group under composition, called the automorphism group of GG, denoted by aut⁡(G)\mathrm{aut}(G).

Lemma C.11.

For nn-vertex graphs, given a pattern graph HH, the global sensitivity GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} is given by

GSfH=(n−2h−2)⋅2​mH​(h−2)!|aut⁡(H)|=Θ⁡(nh−2),\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}=\binom{n-2}{h-2}\cdot\frac{2m_{H}(h-2)!}{|\mathrm{aut}(H)|}=\Theta\left(n^{h-2}\right),

where the hidden constant depends only on hh.

Proof.

Note that GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} is actually the number of occurrences of HH that contain a specific vertex pair (i,j)(i,j) in the complete graph KnK_{n}. This equals the number of ways to choose and permute the remaining h−2h-2 vertices, multiplied by the number of ways to map an edge of HH to (i,j)(i,j), divided by |aut⁡(H)||\mathrm{aut}(H)| to account for symmetries. Since h−1≤mH≤(h2)h-1\leq m_{H}\leq\binom{h}{2} and 1≤|aut⁡(H)|≤h!1\leq|\mathrm{aut}(H)|\leq h!, the expression for GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} yields a tight bound up to constants depending only on hh. ∎

Following analogous reasoning, we can obtain an upper bound for fH​(G)f_{H}(G).

Lemma C.12.

For any nn-vertex graph GG, given a pattern graph HH, it holds that

fH​(G)≤fH​(Kn)=(nh)⋅h!|aut⁡(H)|=Θ⁡(nh),f_{H}(G)\leq f_{H}(K_{n})=\binom{n}{h}\cdot\frac{h!}{|\mathrm{aut}(H)|}=\Theta\left(n^{h}\right),

where the hidden constant depends only on hh.

C.3 Discussions on the approximated local sensitivity HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G)

There is no explicit upper bound on HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G) for all HH, and its value typically varies depending on HH and GG. For some HH, HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G) can be relatively easy to estimate, while for others, it presents more significant challenges. Nevertheless, our results remain practically significant. For convenience, we use △\triangle and ∗* to represent triangle and 22-star in the following lemmas, respectively.

For any constant β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), it holds that HS~f△​(G)≤LSf△​(G)+ln⁡(2/(β​δ′))ε′​(ln⁡(2/(β​δ′))ε′+1)≤dmax​(G)+ln⁡(2/(β​δ′))ε′​(ln⁡(2/(β​δ′))ε′+1)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{\triangle}}(G)\leq\mathrm{LS}_{f_{\triangle}}(G)+\frac{\ln{(2/(\beta\delta^{\prime}))}}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(\frac{\ln{(2/(\beta\delta^{\prime}))}}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}+1)\leq d_{\max}(G)+\frac{\ln{(2/(\beta\delta^{\prime}))}}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}(\frac{\ln{(2/(\beta\delta^{\prime}))}}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}+1) with probability at least 1−β1-\beta.

D.1 Proof of Lemma 2.10

For a matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} with nn columns, and a set S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] we use 𝐀|S\mathbf{A}|_{S} to denote the submatrix of 𝐀\mathbf{A} consisting of the columns corresponding to elements of SS. We adopt the following definition and result from 40, with notation slightly modified. Note that the set CαC_{\alpha} for α=1\alpha=1 is equivalent to the set {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n}.

Definition D.1.

For any 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, we define herdiscCα​(𝐀)=maxS⊆[n]⁡discCα​(𝐀|S).\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=\max\limits_{S\subseteq[n]}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A}|_{S}).

Lemma D.2 (Lemma 5 in 40).

Let f(s)=maxS⊆[n]:|S|≤sdiscCα(𝐀|S).f(s)=\max_{S\subseteq[n]:|S|\leq s}{\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A}|_{S})}. Then discC1​(𝐀)≤∑i=0∞f⁡((1−α)i​n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{A})\leq\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}{f((1-\alpha)^{i}n)}.

The case for d=O⁡(1)d=O(1) Let an anchored axis-parallel box denote an element of the form [0,b0]×⋯×[0,bd][0,b_{0}]\times\cdots\times[0,b_{d}]. By the main results in 39, we obtain the following lemma.

Lemma D.3 (39).

Let d=O⁡(1)d=O(1). For any nn large enough, there exists a set of nn points in [n]d[n]^{d} and nn anchored axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BnB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{n} such that the following holds. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} denote the incidence matrix of the collection of set {Bj∩P,j∈[n]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[n]\}. Then herdiscC1​(𝐀)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{A})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}n).

By an approach similar to that in 40, we derive the following lemma.

Lemma D.4.

Let d=O⁡(1)d=O(1). For any nn large enough, there exists a set of nn points PP and nn axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BnB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{n} with a non-empty common intersection such that the following holds. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} denote the incidence matrix of the collection of set {Bj∩P,j∈[n]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[n]\}. Then for α=Ω⁡(1)\alpha=\Omega(1), discCα​(𝐀)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}n).

Proof.

By Lemma D.3, for any nn large enough, there exists a set of nn points P′P^{\prime} in [n]d[n]^{d} and nn anchored axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BnB_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{n} such that the incidence matrix 𝐁′\mathbf{B}^{\prime} of {Bj∩P′,j∈[n]}\{B_{j}\cap P^{\prime},j\in[n]\} has herdiscC1​(𝐁′)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}n). Note that all boxes BjB_{j} contain the common point (0,0,…,0)(0,0,\dots,0).

Let S∗=arg⁡maxS∈[n]​discC1​(𝐁′|S)S^{*}=\arg\max_{S\in[n]}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime}|_{S}). Let PP be the set of points corresponding to S∗S^{*}, and augment PP with additional points not contained in any of the boxes B1,B2,…,BnB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{n}, so that |P|=n|P|=n. Let 𝐁\mathbf{B} denote the incidence matrix of {Bj∩P,j∈[n]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[n]\}. Then we have discC1​(𝐁)=discC1​(𝐁′|S∗)=herdiscC1​(𝐁′)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B})=\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime}|_{S^{*}})=\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}n).

Now we can prove the lemma. Assume for contradiction that all but finitely many n×nn\times n incidence matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} of points and axis-parallel boxes with a non-empty common intersection have discrepancy discCα​(𝐀)=o⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=o(\log^{d-1}n). We take any set of points PP, axis-parallel boxes, and the corresponding incidence matrix 𝐁\mathbf{B} satisfying discC1​(𝐁)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}n) from the previous construction. By augmenting additional points, any restriction 𝐁|S\mathbf{B}|_{S} for S⊆PS\subseteq P is also the incidence matrix of sets induced by points and axis-parallel boxes in the assumption, and thus we have discCα​(𝐁|S)=o⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{B}|_{S})=o(\log^{d-1}n). Plugging this bound into Lemma D.2, we get discC1​(𝐁)=o⁡(logd−1⁡n)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B})=o(\log^{d-1}n), a contradiction. ∎

The case for d=O⁡(log⁡n)/Ω⁡(log⁡n)d=O(\log n)/\Omega(\log n) A boolean point is a point in {0,1}d\{0,1\}^{d}. A boolean axis-parallel box is an element of {{0},{1},[0,1]}d\{\{0\},\{1\},[0,1]\}^{d}. By a probabilistic construction in 12, we obtain the following lemma.

Lemma D.5 (12).

Let d=Θ⁡(log⁡n)d=\Theta(\log n). For any mm large enough, there exists a set of n=Θ⁡(m)n=\Theta(m) boolean points and mm boolean axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BmB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{m} such that the following holds. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} denote the incidence matrix of the collection of set {Bj∩P,j∈[m]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[m]\}. Then herdiscC1​(𝐀)=nΩ⁡(1)\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{A})=n^{\Omega(1)}.

By a simple transformation and an approach similar to the proof of Lemma D.4, we derive the following lemma.

Lemma D.6.

For any mm large enough, there exists a set of n=Θ⁡(m)n=\Theta(m) points PP and mm axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BmB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{m} with a non-empty common intersection such that the following holds. Let 𝐀\mathbf{A} denote the incidence matrix of the collection of set {Bj∩P,j∈[m]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[m]\}. Then for α=Ω⁡(1)\alpha=\Omega(1),

  • •

    if d=O⁡(log⁡n)d=O(\log n), then discCα​(𝐀)=2Ω⁡(d)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=2^{\Omega(d)};

  • •

    if d=Ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\Omega(\log n), then discCα​(𝐀)=nΩ⁡(1)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=n^{\Omega(1)}.

Proof.

Let d=Θ⁡(log⁡n)d=\Theta(\log n). By Lemma D.5, for any mm large enough, there exists a set of n=Θ⁡(m)n=\Theta(m) boolean points P′P^{\prime} and mm boolean axis-parallel boxes B1′,B2′,…,Bm′B^{\prime}_{1},B^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,B^{\prime}_{m} such that the incidence matrix 𝐁′\mathbf{B}^{\prime} of {Bj′∩P′,j∈[m]}\{B^{\prime}_{j}\cap P^{\prime},j\in[m]\} has herdiscC1​(𝐁′)=nΩ⁡(1)\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime})=n^{\Omega(1)}. Replacing {0}\{0\} and {1}\{1\} in B1′,B2′,…,Bm′B^{\prime}_{1},B^{\prime}_{2},\dots,B^{\prime}_{m} with the intervals [0,0.5][0,0.5] and [0.5,1][0.5,1], respectively, yields axis-parallel boxes B1,B2,…,BmB_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{m}. This transformation preserves the containment of points within boxes, and thus leaves the incidence matrix 𝐁′\mathbf{B}^{\prime} unchanged. Furthermore, all resulting boxes BiB_{i} contain the common point (0.5,0.5,…,0.5)(0.5,0.5,\dots,0.5).

Let S∗=arg⁡maxS∈[n]​discC1​(𝐁′|S)S^{*}=\arg\max_{S\in[n]}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime}|_{S}). Let PP be the set of points corresponding to S∗S^{*}, and augment PP with additional points not contained in any of the boxes B1,B2,…,BmB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{m}, so that |P|=Θ⁡(m)|P|=\Theta(m). Let 𝐁\mathbf{B} denote the incidence matrix of {Bj∩P,j∈[m]}\{B_{j}\cap P,j\in[m]\}. Then we have discC1​(𝐁)=discC1​(𝐁′|S∗)=herdiscC1​(𝐁′)=nΩ⁡(1)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B})=\mathrm{disc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime}|_{S^{*}})=\mathrm{herdisc}_{C_{1}}(\mathbf{B}^{\prime})=n^{\Omega(1)}. Then by an approach similar to the proof of Lemma D.4, we can prove that there are infinitely many m×nm\times n incidence matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} of points and axis-parallel boxes with a non-empty common intersection have discrepancy discCα​(𝐀)=nΩ⁡(1)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=n^{\Omega(1)}.

The case for d=Ω⁡(log⁡n)d=\Omega(\log n) follows immediately from that for d=Θ⁡(log⁡n)d=\Theta(\log n). We thus focus on the case for d=O⁡(log⁡n)d=O(\log n). Set n′=Θ⁡(2d)n^{\prime}=\Theta(2^{d}) so that the above conclusion can be applied to the cases for d=Θ⁡(log⁡n′)d=\Theta(\log n^{\prime}). Let m′m^{\prime} be the number of boxes corresponding to n′n^{\prime}. Then we can add n−n′n-n^{\prime} points that are not contained in any boxes and m−m′m-m^{\prime} boxes that do not contain any points. Thus, we finish the proof of the case for d=O⁡(log⁡n)d=O(\log n). ∎

Combining Lemmas D.4 and D.6, we complete the proof of Lemma 2.10.

E.3 The complexity analysis of the algorithms in Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 3.3

The algorithms in Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 3.3 correspond to Algorithm 3 and Algorithm 5, respectively. Before formally presenting the complexity analysis of these algorithms, we first provide the implementation details about the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} and the range tree in these algorithms, which further reduce the time and space consumption both theoretically and in practice.

Implementation details In practical networks, fH​(G)f_{H}(G) may be significantly lower than the size of the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} in Algorithm 1 (i.e., n2​dn^{2d}). This implies that most components in the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} are 0. Thus, we maintain the non-zero components of 𝐰\mathbf{w} by a hash map to avoid materializing all of [n]2​d[n]^{2d} and employ a dynamic update strategy to implement the range tree more efficiently.

This strategy is based on the observation that the structure of the range tree in Algorithm 2 depends solely on nn and dd, rather than on the specific structure of GG. Moreover, the Laplace noise added to the weight of each tree node is determined before the construction of the range tree in Algorithm 2. Therefore, we can assume that the entire range tree has already been constructed initially, with the weight of each node initialized to 0 and the corresponding Laplace noise added, although this is not actually the case. In other words, each node in the range tree is initially virtual.

Then, each non-zero component in 𝐰\mathbf{w}, whose number is bounded by fH​(G)f_{H}(G), is treated as a modification, incrementing the weight of the relevant tree nodes by 1. During this process, if a node is virtual and is about to be modified, it will be instantiated just before the modification. The process of instantiation includes generating the corresponding Laplace noise and setting the tree node’s weight to the noise value.

Similarly, for any query, the weights of the relevant tree nodes need to be summed. If a queried tree node is virtual, it will be instantiated just before the query.

Now we present the complexity analysis of the above algorithms. Let FH​(G)F_{H}(G) denote the time required to list all occurrences of HH in GG. It is always polynomial since, for any HH, all occurrences can be simply enumerated in O⁡(nh)O(n^{h}) time. In fact, for some specific HH such as a triangle, FH​(G)F_{H}(G) can be improved in sparse graphs (14).

Theorem E.8.

The algorithm in Theorem 3.3 (i.e., Algorithm 3) requires O⁡(min⁡(n2​d,(fH​(G)+|Q|)​log2​d​n))O(\min(n^{2d},(f_{H}(G)+|Q|)\log^{2d}n)) space and O⁡(min⁡(fH​(G),(d​n)2​d)​log2​d​n+FH​(G))O(\min(f_{H}(G),(dn)^{2d})\log^{2d}n+F_{H}(G)) preprocessing time, and each query can be answered in O⁡(log2​d⁡n)O(\log^{2d}n) time. Here, the hidden constants are of the form cO⁡(d)c^{O(d)} for some universal constant c>1c>1.

Proof.

We should decide whether to adopt a dynamic update strategy depending on the specific context.

If so, the space used by Algorithm 3 actually depends on the number of tree nodes accessed during each modification or query, and this number also bounds the query time (see Lemma C.8). Therefore, Algorithm 3 requires O⁡((fH​(G)+|Q|)​log2​d​n)O((f_{H}(G)+|Q|)\log^{2d}n) space and O⁡(fH​(G)​log2​d​n+FH​(G))O(f_{H}(G)\log^{2d}n+F_{H}(G)) preprocessing time by Lemma C.8 since the number of non-zero components of the weight vector 𝐰\mathbf{w} in Algorithm 1 can be bounded by fH​(G)f_{H}(G). Note that querying the same induced subgraph multiple times does not incur additional space; therefore, we retain the previous assumption on QQ in Section 1.1.

Otherwise, since the number of nodes in a 11D range tree is at most (2​n−1)(2n-1), the maximum number of nodes in the 2​d2dD range tree in Algorithm 1 is (2​n−1)2​d(2n-1)^{2d}, obtained by aggregating the results over the 2​d2d dimensions. Therefore, Algorithm 3 requires O⁡(n2​d)O(n^{2d}) space and O⁡((d​n)2​d​log2​d​n+FH​(G))O((dn)^{2d}\log^{2d}n+F_{H}(G)) preprocessing time by Lemma C.7.

Both cases require O⁡(log2​d⁡n)O(\log^{2d}n) query time Lemma C.8. By combining the two cases, the proof is complete. ∎

Theorem E.9.

The algorithm in Theorem 1.3 (i.e., Algorithm 5) requires O⁡(min⁡(n2​d,(fH​(G)+|Q|)​log2​d​n))O(\min(n^{2d},(f_{H}(G)+|Q|)\log^{2d}n)) space and O⁡(n2​mH+min⁡(fH​(G),(d​n)2​d)​log2​d​n+FH​(G))O(n^{2m_{H}}+\min(f_{H}(G),(dn)^{2d})\log^{2d}n+F_{H}(G)) preprocessing time, and each query can be answered in O⁡(log2​d⁡n)O(\log^{2d}n) time. Here, the hidden constants are of the form cO⁡(d)c^{O(d)} for some universal constant c>1c>1.

Proof.

The proof is similar to that of Theorem E.8. The only difference is that Algorithm 5 requires preprocessing HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G) (see Algorithm 4). By Lemma 6 in 42, Algorithm 4 requires O⁡(n2​mH)O(n^{2m_{H}}) time to preprocess HS~fH​(G)\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G). ∎

It is worth noting that the dynamic update strategy ensures that the above algorithms run in polynomial time for d=O⁡(log⁡n/log⁡log⁡n)d=O(\log n/\log\log n). Although the time and space complexity scale exponentially with the dimension and the size of the pattern graph, this limitation reflects the inherent difficulty of range counting and subgraph counting, rather than being specific to our algorithms.

F.2 Proof of Theorem 4.1

The following lemma shows a connection between discrepancy and the reconstruction algorithm, which is similar to Lemma 10 in 40.

Lemma F.2.

For any 𝐱∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, there is a deterministic (not necessarily efficient) algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} given an output 𝐲=ℳ⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}) of some mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} such that ‖𝐲−𝐀H​𝐱H‖∞<12​discCα,H​(𝐀H)\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}_{H}\|_{\infty}<\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}) satisfies ‖𝒜⁡(𝐲)−𝐱‖1≤α​n\|\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}\leq\alpha n.

Proof.

Given 𝐲=ℳ⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}), the algorithm outputs an vector 𝐱′∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that ‖𝐲−𝐀H​𝐱H′‖<12​discCα,H​(𝐀H)\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{H}\|<\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}). Note that such 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} exists, since 𝐱\mathbf{x} already satisfies the required properties. For the sake of contradiction, we assume that ‖𝐱′−𝐱‖1>α​n\|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}>\alpha n. Then χ=𝐱H′−𝐱H\chi=\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{H}-\mathbf{x}_{H} belongs to Cα,HC_{\alpha,H} and therefore ‖𝐀H​χ‖∞≥discCα,H​(𝐀H)\|\mathbf{A}_{H}\chi\|_{\infty}\geq\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}). However, by the triangle inequality, we have ‖𝐀H​χ‖∞≤‖𝐀H​𝐱H′−𝐲‖∞+‖𝐀H​𝐱H−𝐲‖∞<discCα,H​(𝐀H)\|\mathbf{A}_{H}\chi\|_{\infty}\leq\|\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{H}-\mathbf{y}\|_{\infty}+\|\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}_{H}-\mathbf{y}\|_{\infty}<\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}) — a contradiction. ∎

We utilize the following lemma, a simplified version of the result in 18, as a lower bound for RA. This lemma shows that decoding most of the input from the output violates differential privacy.

Lemma F.3 (Lemma 3.9 in 25).

If ℬ\mathcal{B} is an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP reconstruction algorithm for RA and 𝐱\mathbf{x} is uniformly distributed in {0,1}N\{0,1\}^{N}, then we have

𝔼⁡[‖ℬ⁡(𝐱)−𝐱‖1]≥e−ε​(12−δ)​N,\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}]\geq e^{-\varepsilon}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\delta\right)N,

where the expectation is taken over the randomness of both 𝐱\mathbf{x} and ℬ\mathcal{B}.

Finally, we finish the proof of Theorem 4.1.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We first establish that η=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n¯⋅GSfH)\eta=\Omega(\log^{d-1}\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}) for d=O⁡(1)d=O(1).

Let 𝐀,𝐀H,G⁡(𝐱),Q\mathbf{A},\mathbf{A}_{H},G(\mathbf{x}),Q denote the corresponding matrices, graph, and query set, respectively, as defined earlier. Then it holds that discCα​(𝐀)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n¯)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha}}(\mathbf{A})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}\bar{n}) for any constant α\alpha. By Lemma 4.3, it follows that discCα,H​(𝐀H)=Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n¯⋅GSfH)\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H})=\Omega(\log^{d-1}\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}).

For the sake of contradiction, we assume that there exists an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP mechanism ℳ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}) with constants ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈[0,12)\delta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}) for RSC of (3​n−2)(3n-2)-vertex graph relaxed to protect nn private edges, whose additive error is less than 12​discCα,H​(𝐀H)\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\alpha,H}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}) with a sufficiently large constant probability β<1\beta<1.

We apply ℳ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}) to the instance (G⁡(𝐱),Q)(G(\mathbf{x}),Q). By Lemma F.2, there is a deterministic (not necessarily efficient) algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfying ‖𝒜⁡(ℳ⁡(𝐱))−𝐱‖1≤α​n\|\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}))-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}\leq\alpha n for any 𝐱∈{0,1}n\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Let ℬ⁡(𝐱)=𝒜⁡(ℳ⁡(𝐱))\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x})) denote the reconstruction algorithm for RA. By the post-processing property (Proposition C.1), the algorithm ℬ⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x}) preserves (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP. If 𝐱\mathbf{x} is uniformly distributed in {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}, we have 𝔼⁡[‖ℬ⁡(𝐱)−𝐱‖1]≤(β​α+(1−β))​n\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}]\leq(\beta\alpha+(1-\beta))n.

We can always choose a sufficiently small constant α>0\alpha>0 and a sufficiently large constant β<1\beta<1 such that 𝔼⁡[‖ℬ⁡(𝐱)−𝐱‖1]<e−ε​(12−δ)​n\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{B}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}]<e^{-\varepsilon}(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n, which yields a contradiction with Lemma F.3.

By appropriately rescaling and GSfH=Θ⁡(nh−2)\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}=\Theta(n^{h-2}) (see Lemma C.11), we can obtain the same lower bound for DPRSC of nn-vertex graphs.

Now consider the case for d=ω⁡(1)d=\omega(1). The proofs for d=O⁡(log⁡n¯)d=O(\log\bar{n}) and d=Ω⁡(log⁡n¯)d=\Omega(\log\bar{n}) follow by applying the same techniques as that for d=O⁡(1)d=O(1). ∎

F.4 A lower bound for the case d=1d=1

By combining our approach with the method of 23, we obtain a lower bound for DPRSC with d=1d=1. When |Q|≥nc|Q|\geq n^{c} for any sufficiently small constant c>0c>0, a similar lower bound Ω⁡(log⁡n⋅HS~fH​(G))\Omega(\log n\cdot\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G)) follows from the following theorem and the proof of Theorem 1.4.

Theorem F.4.

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0 be a constant and δ=n−Ω⁡(1)\delta=n^{-\Omega(1)}. For any pattern graph HH, let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm for the range subgraph counting problem with additive error η=maxq∈Q⁡|fH​(Gq)−f~H​(Gq)|\eta=\max_{q\in Q}|f_{H}(G_{q})-\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})| with probability at least 23\frac{2}{3}.

Then there exist infinitely many nn-vertex graphs G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}) with 11-dimensional vertex attributes and a corresponding query set QQ, such that η=Ω⁡(log⁡n¯⋅GSfH)\eta=\Omega(\log\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}), where n¯=min⁡(n,|Q|)\bar{n}=\min(n,|Q|) can be arbitrarily large.

Proof.

Let PP denote a set of n¯\bar{n} vertices, where the attribute of the ii-th vertex is ii for all i∈[n¯]i\in[\bar{n}]. Let QQ denote a set of n¯\bar{n} intervals, where the ii-th interval is [0,i][0,i] for all i∈[n¯]i\in[\bar{n}]. We can always adjust the size of PP by adding n−n¯n-\bar{n} dummy points lying outside all boxes in QQ, or adjust the size of QQ by adding |Q|−n¯|Q|-\bar{n} dummy intervals not containing any points. Therefore, it suffices to analyze the case for |P|=n|P|=n and |Q|=n¯|Q|=\bar{n}.

Note that all intervals in QQ share a common intersection at 0. We construct an (3​n−2)(3n-2)-vertex graph G⁡(𝐱)G(\mathbf{x}) based on PP and QQ as Section 4.1. Assume that δ∈[0,n−c)\delta\in[0,n^{-c}) for some small constant c>0c>0. Let k=c1​ln⁡n¯k=c_{1}\ln\bar{n} for a constant c1∈(0,min⁡(1,c)2​ε)c_{1}\in(0,\frac{\min(1,c)}{2\varepsilon}).

Let GSfH\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} denote the global sensitivity of fHf_{H} on nn-vertex graphs. For the sake of contradiction, assume that there exists an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for RSC of (3​n−2)(3n-2)-vertex graph relaxed to protect nn private edges. The algorithm achieves additive error at most c2​ln⁡n¯⋅GSfHc_{2}\ln\bar{n}\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}} with probability at least 23\frac{2}{3}, where c2c_{2} is a constant with c2∈(0,c16)c_{2}\in(0,\frac{c_{1}}{6}).

Appendix G Deferred Experiments from Section 5

G.1 Deferred experiments when HH is an edge

In this subsection, we present the experimental results when HH is an edge. Figures 8, 8, 10 and 10 report the relationship between the relative error and ε\varepsilon, the relationship between the relative error and |Q||Q|, the query time and preprocessing time, and the total time, respectively.

For edge counting, Algorithm 4 used in ADP_comp and ADP_RSC is meaningless since the global sensitivity is 1. In practice, we directly use GSfH=1\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}=1 and apply the advanced composition theorem (Proposition 2.4). The baselines require no preprocessing time for similar reasons and compute exact counts of edges using a straightforward implementation in O⁡(m)O(m) time. The experimental results obtained are similar to those presented in Section 5.

G.2 Deferred experiments when d>1d>1

We report results for the case d>1d>1 on the relatively small CA-Netscience dataset in this subsection. Due to the increased computational cost, experiments on larger datasets become prohibitively expensive. We set |Q|=n2|Q|=n^{2} and compare the cases for d=1,2d=1,2 as shown in Figures 14, 14, 14 and 14.

These figures show that both the additive error and the runtime of our algorithms increase significantly as dd grows, with the observed scaling largely matching our theoretical analysis. While our algorithms no longer outperform the baselines on this dataset when d=2d=2, the behavior is consistent with our theoretical expectations: although our method improves the asymptotic dependence, its advantage only becomes apparent in regimes where nn and |Q||Q| are large. Additionally, we observe that our approximate DP algorithm exhibits a more pronounced advantage over the pure DP algorithm when d=2d=2, consistent with their different constant factors in the exponent with respect to dd in Theorems 1.3 and 3.3.

G.3 Deferred experiments for small-range queries

In this subsection, we report results for small-range queries with |Vq|=O⁡(|Q|)|V_{q}|=O(\sqrt{|Q|}) on WormNet-v3, and show the additive error with respect to ε\varepsilon in Figure 15. We observe that our algorithms maintain a significant advantage over the baselines on small-range queries. Meanwhile, both the mean and variance of the relative error increase substantially for all methods, due to the reduced magnitude and higher variability of the true answers in this regime.

G.4 Deferred implementation details and experiments for real attributes

We note that in many real-world applications, attributes often exhibit significant redundancy, with many duplicate values along each dimension. In such cases, the effective domain size per attribute is small, which can, in fact, improve the performance of our algorithms. In contrast, the setting with independently sampled continuous attributes represents a more challenging regime, where the values in each attribute dimension are almost surely all distinct. Thus, the setting used in the main text can be viewed as a conservative (worst-case) evaluation of our algorithms.

From a theoretical perspective, this observation can be made precise. The analysis of both the additive error and the time and space complexity can be refined to depend on the effective domain size of each attribute. In particular, the factor logO⁡(d)⁡n\log^{O(d)}n can be replaced by (∏i=1d(⌈log⁡|Ai​(V,𝐚)|⌉+1))O⁡(1)(\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\lceil\log|A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a})|\rceil+1))^{O(1)}, where Ai​(V,𝐚)A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a}) denotes the set of distinct values of the ii-th attribute (as defined before Definition 3.1). This refinement follows from the fact that the rank si​(v)s_{i}(v) in Section 3 naturally takes values in [|Ai​(V,𝐚)|][|A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a})|] rather than [n][n]. Consequently, the dependence on log⁡n\log n in the noise parameters of our algorithms can be replaced by (⌈log⁡|Ai​(V,𝐚)|⌉+1)(\lceil\log|A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a})|\rceil+1), yielding improved bounds for both the additive error and the time and space complexity. In particular, by a minor adaptation of the proofs of Theorems 1.3 and E.9, we obtain the following corollary. A similar corollary can also be derived from Theorems 3.3 and E.8.

Corollary G.1.

Let L⁡(V,𝐚)=∏i=1d(⌈log⁡|Ai​(V,𝐚)|⌉+1)L(V,\mathbf{a})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(\lceil\log|A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a})|\rceil+1) and M⁡(V,𝐚)=∏i=1d(2​|Ai​(V,𝐚)|−1)M(V,\mathbf{a})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(2|A_{i}(V,\mathbf{a})|-1). For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there exists a (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm that, given a graph G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}) with dd-dimensional vertex attributes, a fixed pattern graph HH, and a query set QQ, outputs noisy answers f~H​(Gq)\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q}) which satisfy

maxq∈Q⁡|fH​(Gq)−f~H​(Gq)|=O⁡(HS~fH​(G)⋅(ε+log⁡(1/δ))​log⁡(n​|Q|)⋅L2​(V,𝐚)ε)\displaystyle\max_{q\in Q}\left|f_{H}(G_{q})-\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})\right|=O\left(\frac{\widetilde{\mathrm{HS}}_{f_{H}}(G)\cdot\sqrt{(\varepsilon+\log(1/\delta))\log(n|Q|)}\cdot L^{2}(V,\mathbf{a})}{\varepsilon}\right)

with probability at least 1−1n1-\frac{1}{n}. The algorithm requires O⁡(min⁡(M2​(V,𝐚),(fH​(G)+|Q|)​L2​(V,𝐚)))O(\min(M^{2}(V,\mathbf{a}),(f_{H}(G)+|Q|)L^{2}(V,\mathbf{a}))) space and O⁡(min⁡(fH​(G)​L2​(V,𝐚),M2​(V,𝐚)​log2​d​M2​(V,𝐚))+FH​(G))O(\min(f_{H}(G)L^{2}(V,\mathbf{a}),M^{2}(V,\mathbf{a})\log^{2d}M^{2}(V,\mathbf{a}))+F_{H}(G)) preprocessing time, and each query can be answered in O​(L2​(V,𝐚))O(L^{2}(V,\mathbf{a})) time. Here, the hidden constants are of the form cO⁡(d)c^{O(d)} for some universal constant c>1c>1.

Due to the scarcity of suitable real-world graph datasets with attributes aligned with our setting, we conduct experiments on Wiki-Squirrel with real attributes satisfying |A1​(V,𝐚)|=2002|A_{1}(V,\mathbf{a})|=2002. We present the results in Figures 19, 19, 19 and 19. These figures show that our algorithms remain significantly better than the baselines for real attributes. Moreover, due to the smaller effective domain size, our algorithms achieve substantially improved performance compared to the setting where attributes are independently sampled from a standard normal distribution, which is consistent with our theoretical analysis.

H.1 Randomized response method

In this subsection, we show that by using the randomized response, we obtain polynomial-time DP algorithms for range subgraph counting. Let 𝟏k\mathbf{1}_{k} denote the kk-bit all-ones vector.

Definition H.1 (Randomized Response, 36; 48).

Given a privacy parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0 and a kk-bit vector v, the algorithm RRε​(v)\mathrm{RR}_{\varepsilon}(\textbf{v}) outputs a kk-bit vector, where for each i∈[k]i\in[k], bit ii is viv_{i} with probability eεeε+1\frac{e^{\varepsilon}}{e^{\varepsilon}+1} and 1−vi1-v_{i} otherwise.

Lemma H.2.

Randomized Response is an ε\varepsilon-DP.

We apply a linear transformation to the output of randomized response and obtain an unbiased estimation of the input vector, which is described in Algorithm 6. Our subsequent algorithms mainly rely on the result of Algorithm 6.

Algorithm 6 is a ε\varepsilon-DP and returns an unbiased estimate of the input vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}.

A sequence of real-valued random variables Z0,Z1,…,ZtZ_{0},Z_{1},\dots,Z_{t} is a martingale with respect to a sequence of random variables ξ1,…,ξt\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{t} if for all i∈[t]i\in[t], it holds that 𝔼[Zi∣ξ1,…,ξi−1]=Zi−1\mathbb{E}[Z_{i}\mid\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{i-1}]=Z_{i-1}.

H.1.2 The second bound

For moderate |Q||Q| (i.e., |Q|=2no⁡(1)|Q|=2^{n^{o(1)}}), we extend the methods in 25 and obtain an instance-dependent error for the private range subgraph counting problem. We sketch the analysis in this subsection and present the entire algorithm in Algorithm 8.

For any two sets AA and BB, define their symmetric difference as A​△​B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A)A\triangle B=(A\setminus B)\cup(B\setminus A). Given two graphs G1=(V1,E1)G_{1}=(V_{1},E_{1}) and G2=(V2,E2)G_{2}=(V_{2},E_{2}), their symmetric difference is defined as G1​△​G2=(V1∪V2,E1​△​E2)G_{1}\triangle G_{2}=(V_{1}\cup V_{2},E_{1}\triangle E_{2}). We write G1≅G2G_{1}\cong G_{2} if graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are isomorphic. For a fixed graph HH and an integer i∈[mH]i\in[m_{H}], let 𝒢H(i)\mathcal{G}_{H}^{(i)} denote the class of graphs that can be obtained as the symmetric difference of two isomorphic copies H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} of HH whose edge sets intersect in exactly ii edges, i.e., 𝒢H(i)={H1△H2∣H1,H2≅H,|E(H1)∩E(H2)|=i}\mathcal{G}_{H}^{(i)}=\{\,H_{1}\triangle H_{2}\mid H_{1},H_{2}\cong H,\;|E(H_{1})\cap E(H_{2})|=i\,\}. Then we have the following theorem.

Theorem H.7.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 , there exists a polynomial-time ε\varepsilon-DP algorithm that, given a graph G=(V,E,𝐚)G=(V,E,\mathbf{a}), where the attribute of each vertex is a dd-dimensional vector (d=no⁡(1)d=n^{o(1)}), a pattern graph HH, a query set QQ, outputs all range subgraph counting queries which satisfy

maxq∈Q⁡|fH​(Gq)−f~H​(Gq)|=O⁡((τε)mH​nh2+∑i=1mH−1(τε)i​∑H′∈𝒢H(i)fH′​(G))\max_{q\in Q}\left|f_{H}(G_{q})-\widetilde{f}_{H}(G_{q})\right|=O\left(\left(\frac{\tau}{\varepsilon}\right)^{m_{H}}n^{\frac{h}{2}}+\sum_{i=1}^{m_{H}-1}\left(\frac{\tau}{\varepsilon}\right)^{i}\sum_{H^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}_{H}^{(i)}}\sqrt{f_{H^{\prime}}(G)}\right)

with probability at least 1−1n1-\frac{1}{n}, where τ=log⁡(n​|Q|)≤O⁡(d​log⁡n)\tau=\log(n|Q|)\leq O(d\log n).

Let G⁡(n,p)G(n,p) denote the distribution of Erdős–Rényi random graphs. For any graph G=(V,E)∼G⁡(n,p)G=(V,E)\sim G(n,p), we use the following lemma to bound the number of occurrences of HH in GG containing each edge e∈Ee\in E.

Lemma H.11.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph generated from G⁡(n,p)G(n,p). If p≫((ln⁡n)/n)1/(2​mH−2)p\gg\left((\ln n)/n\right)^{1/(2m_{H}-2)} or HH is an edge (i.e., mH=1m_{H}=1), with probability at least 1−poly⁡(1/n)1-\mathrm{poly}(1/n), the following properties (⋆)(\star) hold:

  1. 1.

    for each vertex v∈Vv\in V, its degree belongs to the interval [γ​n2,2​γ​n][\frac{\gamma n}{2},2\gamma n];

  2. 2.

    for each e∈Ee\in E, the number of occurrences of HH containing ee belongs to the interval [LSfH​(G)2,2​LSfH​(G)][\frac{\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)}{2},2\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)] and LSfH​(G)=Θ⁡(GSfH⋅pmH−1)\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)=\Theta(\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1}).

Proof.

Item 1 in the properties (⋆)(\star) follows from the Chernoff bound. We now focus on Item 2. Note that when h=2h=2 and mH=1m_{H}=1 (i.e., HH is an edge), it holds automatically since LSfH​(G)=1\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)=1. Therefore, we assume h≥3h\geq 3 and mH≥2m_{H}\geq 2 in the following. Fix an edge e∈Ee\in E. Let XeX_{e} denote the number of occurrences of HH containing ee in GG. Fix an arbitrary ordering of the edges in {(u,v)∣u,v∈V}∖{e}\{(u,v)\mid u,v\in V\}\setminus\{e\}, denoted by e1,e2,…,e(n2)−1e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{\binom{n}{2}-1}, and define the indicator random variable Yi=𝟙ei∈EY_{i}=\mathds{1}_{e_{i}\in E} for each i∈[(n2)−1]i\in[\binom{n}{2}-1]. Let Z0=𝔼⁡[Xe]=GSfH⋅pmH−1Z_{0}=\mathbb{E}[X_{e}]=\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1}. For each i∈[(n2)−1]i\in[\binom{n}{2}-1], let Zi=𝔼[Xe|Y1,…,Yi]Z_{i}=\mathbb{E}[X_{e}|Y_{1},\dots,Y_{i}]. Then Z(n2)−1=XeZ_{\binom{n}{2}-1}=X_{e} and Z0,…,Z(n2)−1Z_{0},\dots,Z_{\binom{n}{2}-1} is a martingale by the law of total expectation.

By an analysis similar to the proof of Lemma C.11, for each edge eie_{i}, if it shares an endpoint with ee, then |Zi−Zi−1|≤Θ⁡(nh−3)|Z_{i}-Z_{i-1}|\leq\Theta(n^{h-3}); otherwise, |Zi−Zi−1|≤Θ⁡(nh−4)|Z_{i}-Z_{i-1}|\leq\Theta(n^{h-4}). By Lemma C.11 and Lemma H.5, if p≫((ln⁡n)/n)1/(2​mH−2)p\gg((\ln n)/n)^{1/(2m_{H}-2)}, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

exp⁡(−(ε⋅GSfH⋅pmH−1)22​(∑i=1(n2)−1ci2))≤exp⁡(−C⋅n2​h−4⋅p2​mH−22​n⋅n2​h−6+n2⋅n2​h−8)≤poly⁡(1/n).\exp\left(-\frac{(\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1})^{2}}{2\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\binom{n}{2}-1}c_{i}^{2}\right)}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{C\cdot n^{2h-4}\cdot p^{2m_{H}-2}}{2n\cdot n^{2h-6}+n^{2}\cdot n^{2h-8}}\right)\leq\mathrm{poly}(1/n).

Then with probability at least 1−poly⁡(1/n)1-\mathrm{poly}(1/n), XeX_{e} belongs to the interval [(1−ε)​GSfH⋅pmH−1,(1+ε)​GSfH⋅pmH−1][(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1},(1+\varepsilon)\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1}] for some ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Note that LSfH​(G)=maxe∈E⁡Xe\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)=\max_{e\in E}X_{e}. By the union bound and choosing a suitable constant ε>0\varepsilon>0, it holds that with probability at least 1−poly⁡(1/n)1-\mathrm{poly}(1/n), all the random variables XeX_{e} lie in the interval [LSfH​(G)2, 2​LSfH​(G)][\frac{\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)}{2},\,2\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)] and LSfH​(G)=Θ⁡(GSfH⋅pmH−1)\mathrm{LS}_{f_{H}}(G)=\Theta\left(\mathrm{GS}_{f_{H}}\cdot p^{m_{H}-1}\right). By the union bound, with probability at least 1−poly⁡(1/n)1-\mathrm{poly}(1/n), the properties (⋆)(\star) are satisfied. ∎

Lemma H.12.

Let 𝐱\mathbf{x} be the indicator vector of the edge set of some graph GG satisfying the properties (⋆\star) in Lemma H.11. There is a deterministic algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} given an output 𝐲=ℳ⁡(𝐱)\mathbf{y}=\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{x}) of some mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} such that ‖𝐲−𝐀H​𝐱H‖∞<12​discCσ,γ​(𝐀H)\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{A}_{H}\mathbf{x}_{H}\|_{\infty}<\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{disc}_{C_{\sigma,\gamma}}(\mathbf{A}_{H}) satisfies ‖𝒜⁡(𝐲)−𝐱‖1≤σ​γ​n2\|\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y})-\mathbf{x}\|_{1}\leq\sigma\gamma n^{2}.

Let ℳ:𝒳→ℛ\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{R} be an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private mechanism, c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N}, and 𝐱,𝐱′∈𝒳\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} such that ‖𝐱−𝐱′‖1≤c\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\|_{1}\leq c.
